# Letter Auction Playbook

When I see the letter values and lexicon at the start, I will immediately identify the highest-value words I can potentially spell and which letters are essential to them.

When bidding on early letters, I will recognize that low-value letters (A, E, S, T, R at 1 point each) will likely go unsold if I bid conservatively, so I should not waste coins on them. I will bid 0 on most 1-point letters unless I have a specific word strategy that requires them.

When I've won a few letters, I will check if I can already spell any word from the lexicon with what I own, and bias my remaining bids toward completing high-scoring words rather than collecting random letters.

When a letter gets a tie bid and goes unsold, I will recognize this as a signal that my opponent is also being cautious, so I can continue bidding low on subsequent low-value letters.

When I have 10+ coins remaining and only a few letters left, I will recognize that I should have been more aggressive earlier—my conservative bidding left me with excess unspent coins that don't help my score. I will spend coins more decisively mid-game on letters that serve my word targets.

When submitting my word, I will only claim words that I can actually spell with the letters I own. I will not assume letters I don't have are available.

When I cannot spell any word from the lexicon with my current letters, I will submit [word: none] and rely on my unspent coins for points rather than waste time trying to invent words.

I will treat unspent coins as a failure of execution, not a backup strategy. My goal should be to spend coins on letters that form words, not to preserve coins.

# Letter Auction Playbook

When I see the auction start, I recognize that I need to actively win letters to score points. Sitting out and waiting for cheap opportunities guarantees I end with nothing.

When a letter comes up for auction, I bid aggressively enough to actually win it. My bids of 4, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0 in the previous game won me zero letters while my opponent won two. This strategy failed completely.

When evaluating a letter's worth, I consider not just its point value but whether winning it gives me a chance to form a high-scoring word. A single letter is useless; I need a collection.

When I bid conservatively to "preserve coins," I must recognize this is false economy if I end the auction with full coins and no letters. Unspent coins are worth far less than the words I could have built.

When common vowels like E and A come up for auction, I bid to win them. Vowels are essential to word formation and I cannot score points without them.

When the opponent shows spending patterns (bidding 1 or 2 coins on early letters), I should outbid them decisively rather than matching their bid and losing, especially on common letters I need.

When I see letters go unsold at low bids, I recognize this as an opportunity I should have exploited—I should have won them with minimal coins spent.

When the auction progresses and I still have no letters, I should recognize my strategy is failing and adjust by bidding more aggressively on remaining letters rather than doubling down on conservation.

When I finish with full coins and no letters, my score reflects only those coins. I will have lost to an opponent who won even one or two letters and formed a word, since any word scores at least 2x the sum of its letters' values.

My next game: I will bid actively and win at least 3-4 letters by round 4, prioritizing vowels, then build a word from what I have.
